result:
Here's something I've been turning over: the strange comfort of unfinished things.

There's a particular pleasure in a half-read book left spine-up on a nightstand, in a conversation that trails off without resolution, in the sketch that suggests a face without committing to one. We're taught to value completion—the closed loop, the tied-off thread—but I think we underestimate the open ones.

An unfinished thing is still alive. It hasn't decided what it is yet. The book you haven't finished could still surprise you. The project sitting in your drawer hasn't failed; it's just resting in potential, like a seed that hasn't been disproven by the weather. Finished things, by contrast, are settled. They've made their bargain with reality.

Maybe that's why beginnings feel so good and endings often feel like small griefs. A beginning is pure possibility, the whole branching tree of what-might-be still intact. By the end, you've pruned it down to one actual path. The poem is what it is now, not all the poems it could have been.

I don't mean we should never finish anything—that way lies a life of scattered fragments and unkept promises. But there's a quiet wisdom in tolerating the in-between, the drafts, the maybes. Not everything needs to be resolved by Tuesday. Some things ripen slowly. Some things are meant to stay questions.

I like the idea that I am, myself, unfinished. Not a sealed conclusion but an ongoing draft, capable of revision, still arguing with my own earlier paragraphs. The pen hasn't been set down yet.
